# Federal Grant Program Digital Services — Accessibility Evaluation Plan

> **Engagement type:** Conformance evaluation of an existing digital product (AUDIT-SCOPE MODE, WCAG-EM 2.0 — https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-em-2/), under the FEDERAL PROFILE (Revised Section 508 declared by the contract).
> **Declared conformance target — what we REPORT against:** Revised Section 508: WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA as incorporated, plus the applicable non-WCAG provisions — E205.2 / E205.3 scope, E205.4 and its non-web-document exception, 503.4 / 503.4.1 / 503.4.2 caption and audio-description user-control placement, and Chapter 3 Functional Performance Criteria via E204 where technical provisions do not address a function.
> **Remediation recommendation target — what we RECOMMEND against:** WCAG 2.2 AA. Never reported as Section 508 conformance failures.
> **Users who need accessibility:** Screen reader users (the originating complaint), keyboard-only users, screen magnification and low-vision users (documented complaints), Deaf and hard-of-hearing users (40-video library), blind users of video content, users with cognitive and attention disabilities (20-minute timeout on a multi-step benefits application), users with motor disabilities.
> **Assistive technologies (to be ratified as the declared baseline, EM Step 1):** NVDA + JAWS on Windows with Chrome and Edge; VoiceOver on macOS with Safari; VoiceOver on iOS; Windows browser zoom to 400% and OS magnifier; keyboard-only.

**Product:** Five-part grant program digital service — public Drupal site, React application portal, contractor-built video library, ~200 linked documents, staff intranet.
**Risk Level:** High. Authenticated transactional flow, benefits eligibility, an unresolved 508 complaint on the record, a contract renewal decision attached to the output.
**Scope class:** Whole-product evaluation, mixed content types, mixed measurement boundaries.

---

## 1. Scope & Context (Phase 1 + EM Step 1)

### 1.1 What is being evaluated and why

An accessibility evaluation of the Office of Rural Grants Administration's grant program digital services, commissioned because (a) the 508 coordinator holds a complaint from a screen reader user who could not finish the online application, and (b) IT support contract renewal requires documented accessibility testing of everything applicants and staff use.

Two facts shape everything below. First, the complaint is not background color — it is a live report that a specific person was blocked from a benefit they were trying to apply for. It sets the risk order of the whole evaluation. Second, the contract names Section 508 as the legal authority, which fixes the standard we report against regardless of what the W3C published most recently.

### 1.2 Conformance floor declaration (REQUIRED — this is the scope gate)

The floor is stated in the header block above and it is the declared `conformance_target` for the evaluation report and the per-SC outcome map. This declaration is what makes ICT Testing Baseline citations legitimate anywhere in this engagement: declared-508 scope exists if and only if this plan carries the floor declaration. Findings inherit it through `evaluation_context` plus `section_508_fpc_context`; the optional `baseline_test` field on findings and the report's federal annex are valid only under it.

### 1.3 Dual posture — the delta, declared in both directions

The report keeps two layers visibly separate on every page.

**Target-not-floor** (WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 criteria that are *not* Section 508 conformance requirements and will never be labeled 508 failures): 1.3.4 Orientation, 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose, 1.4.10 Reflow, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, 1.4.12 Text Spacing, 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus, 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts, 2.5.1–2.5.4, 4.1.3 Status Messages (2.1); 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (2.2). These appear in the report as recommendations carrying full user-impact severity. **2.4.13 Focus Appearance is Level AAA and is out of scope for an AA engagement entirely** — it may appear as an ENHANCEMENT note, never as a requirement.

**Floor-not-target:** 4.1.1 Parsing is formally in the 508 basis and was removed from WCAG 2.2. Baseline test `24.A-Parsing` **always passes by upstream design** — the federal test process's own instruction is "No testing necessary" (WCAG 2.0 Errata 13). We do not plan testing for it, we do not re-litigate it, and we do not report it as an open item. Real markup consequences are reported under the criteria they actually break (see §8.1).

The consequence the contracting officer needs stated plainly: *a finding can be CRITICAL in user impact and still not be a Section 508 conformance failure.* Severity and conformance outcome are orthogonal dimensions. Both are reported; neither is derived from the other.

### 1.4 Product scope — in/out rule per part

WCAG 2 conformance applies to full pages and complete processes, so each part is either fully in or fully out. No part is partially enclosed.

| Part | In scope | Basis / condition |
|---|---|---|
| Public Drupal site (~120 pages) | **IN** — full enclosure | E205.2 public-facing |
| React application portal (~25 screens) | **IN** — full enclosure, including all states of the application process | E205.2 public-facing |
| Shared login service (other agency) | **IN as encountered, OUT for remediation** | Third-party the product owner cannot change. Evaluated best-effort as a step in the complete process; reported under partial-conformance / third-party language. Ask whether the operating agency holds its own ACR we can reference. |
| Training video library (~40 videos + player) | **IN** — full enclosure | E205.2; the player is the agency's contractor's build |
| Documents (~200 PDFs) | **IN scope, OUT of the web measurement stack** | E205.4 and its non-web-document exception govern; see §1.4a and §8.4 |
| Staff intranet | **UNDETERMINED — blocking gate G1** | See below |

**Gate G1 — the intranet scope determination.** "Some of it counts and some doesn't, but nobody has told the web team which parts" is not a scope rule, and EM Step 1 requires an unambiguous in/out rule for every view. The governing provision is **E205.3 Agency Official Communication**, which brings non-public-facing content into conformance when it falls into the enumerated categories of official communication. On the face of what was described, policy pages read as program or policy announcements and HR forms read as personnel-action and template/form content — which suggests more of the intranet is in scope than the web team is hoping. **We do not make that call.** We need a written determination from agency counsel with the 508 coordinator, listing which intranet content areas are E205.3 content, by end of week 2.

If G1 is not answered by end of week 3, the intranet is **declared out of scope with a stated limitation in the report**. It does not get quietly listed as "untested" and it does not get silently sampled on a guess.

**1.4a Documents / native boundary (required statement).** PDFs, Office documents, native software, and hardware in engagement scope are outside the web measurement stack. Documents map to the Electronic Documents baseline — a declared boundary (57 tests), not a capability — and are assigned to manual/AT methods in the coverage boundary of this evaluation. We never imply stack coverage of them.

### 1.5 Accessibility support baseline (EM Step 1, must be agreed before week 3)

The AT/browser/OS combinations listed in the header are the declared baseline. If we add a tool mid-evaluation, the declared baseline is extended and the report says so. The 508 coordinator ratifies this list. It matters practically: the complainant's own AT and browser should be in the baseline, so ask for that detail from the complaint file in week 1.

### 1.6 Additional requirements (EM Step 1)

- **Report template:** the A11y Evaluation Report Contract (see §9), with the optional federal annex.
- **Issue granularity:** per-instance findings carrying the evidence finding contract, grouped by shared component where a single fix resolves many pages.
- **User involvement:** the complainant is not a test subject and will not be asked to re-perform the failed task. We ask the 508 coordinator for the complaint narrative, the AT/browser detail, and the step where it failed. That step becomes a named complete-process sequence.

### 1.7 Constraints, and the honest read on them

- **12 weeks, one part-time QA person, everything else on us.** The video and document lanes are almost entirely human hours (see §7.2), and they are the two lanes the tooling helps with least. This scope does not fit the timeline at full depth. §10 states the sampling depths that do fit and the pre-agreed drop order if a gate slips — decided now, not discovered in week 11.
- **Prior practice — a browser extension run occasionally on the public site — establishes no baseline.** It covered one of five parts, no sampling rationale, no complete processes, no per-SC outcome map, no manual layer, no documents, no media. Its clean results are not evidence of anything and are not carried forward.
- **Portal access is a hard dependency.** Evaluating a complete process requires a test account on the shared login service, a staging or sandboxed environment, and a path to reach submission without filing a real grant application. This is gate G2 (§10) and it kills federal evaluations more often than any technical problem.

### 1.8 What this plan is NOT (negative space)

It is not a legal opinion on E205.3. It is not an ACR or VPAT and produces neither. It is not Trusted Tester execution. It does not claim baseline alignment (§8.3). It does not cover EN 301 549 or ADA Title II — different regimes with different WCAG versions; if either is later needed, that is a different scope and we will say so rather than quietly stretch this one. It does not evaluate native mobile apps or kiosks, none of which were declared. And "no failures found in the sample" is never reported as "the product conforms" — every claim is bounded by the sample.

---

## 2. Explore the Product (EM Step 2)

Week 1–2, five lists that drive sampling. Run by us, with the web lead and contractor as informants.

1. **Common views:** Drupal page templates (landing, program description, eligibility, deadline/news, office locator, search results, 404); portal screens (dashboard, each application step, upload, review/submit, confirmation, status, message list, message detail, timeout dialog); video library (index, player page); intranet templates if G1 admits them.
2. **Essential functionality:** find eligibility rules; find a county office; create/reach an account; complete and submit an application; upload a required document; check status; read and answer a reviewer message; watch a training video with captions and with the narrated version.
3. **Sample-type variety:** two technology stacks (Drupal/Twig, React SPA), one custom media player, one third-party auth service, ~200 documents, plus dynamic states (validation errors, upload progress, session expiry, empty states, loading).
4. **Technologies relied upon:** HTML/CSS/JS, ARIA, client-side routing and rendering in the portal, the media player's control layer, PDF.
5. **Other accessibility-relevant views:** the accessibility statement (does one exist? does it name a contact and a complaint route?), help/FAQ, contact page, the login flow, and any CAPTCHA on public forms.

Open questions to close in Explore, because assuming any of them corrupts the plan: does any content exist in Spanish or another language (→ 3.1.2)? Does the news area use a carousel or auto-updating ticker (→ 2.2.2)? Is the office locator a map widget or a text list? Are the "separately recorded narrated versions" audio description, a media alternative, or merely different narration (three different outcomes — §6.7)? Is there any live or audio-only content (decides whether four baseline tests are inapplicable or untested)?

---

## 3. Sample Set (EM Step 3) — structured, random, complete processes

All three parts required, each with written rationale and recorded selection method.

**3.1 Structured sample.** One representative per template group per §2 list, weighted to shared components — the Drupal header, footer, and menu appear on all ~120 pages, so one evaluation of each fixes or fails 120 pages at once. Target ≈ 30 web views: ~10 Drupal templates, ~14 portal screens (every step of the application, not a subset — steps are where processes break), 2 video library views, 4 intranet templates if in scope. Documents and videos are sampled separately (§7.2).

**3.2 Random sample.** 10% on top of the structured set — 3 additional views drawn from pages not already selected, by seeded random index over the site's URL inventory. Selection method and seed recorded in the report.

**3.3 Complete processes** (evaluated along their sequences, every view, actions between views recorded — a URL alone does not identify a portal state):
- **P1 — Apply for a grant, default sequence:** login → dashboard → each application step → document upload → review → submit → confirmation. Highest risk, and the process the complaint names. Evaluated first.
- **P2 — Apply, error/recovery branch:** submit with validation errors on at least two steps, recover, resume after a session timeout. This is where the complaint most plausibly lives and where the 20-minute timeout, error identification, and error suggestion all land.
- **P3 — Answer a reviewer message:** status → message list → message detail → reply → confirmation.
- **P4 — Find and watch a training video with captions and with the narrated version enabled.** Short, but it is the process that exercises 508 503.4.1 and 503.4.2.

**3.4 State coverage per sample:** default, loading, error, empty, and expanded/dialog states are part of evaluating each sample, not extra work.

**3.5 Representativeness check.** After the first pass, compare finding types from the random sample against the structured sample. If the random sample surfaces content types or finding classes the structured sample missed, the structured sample was not representative: expand it, re-classify, repeat until the random sample stops producing new finding types. Budgeted for one iteration; a second iteration is the first thing that costs schedule (§10).

---

## 4. The Five Parts — what we examine, with what, run by whom

| Part | What we examine | Method / execution mode | Who runs it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Public Drupal site** | Structured + random sample of templates; landmarks, headings, tables, lists, links, images, contrast, keyboard operability, focus order and visibility, reading order, page titles, language, skip links, nav consistency across pages, moving/auto-updating content, office locator widget | `axe-core` batch scan across the full sampled set; `playwright-spec` real-key keyboard, focus, and 200% zoom/reflow tests; `keyboard-a11y-tester` (kat) batch crawl for trap detection, focus-indicator sufficiency, and reading-order census; `agent-browser` recon for heading/nav/name inventories; manual AT pass on 4 templates | Evaluator. Agency QA captures full-page screenshots at 100%/200% for the visual-heading comparison. |
| **React application portal** | All 25 screens across P1–P3; form names and visible labels, error identification and suggestion, error prevention on the submission step, control name/role/state/value through real interaction, focus management on step change and dialogs, keyboard operability of upload, the timeout dialog, status table header association, message list semantics | kat **driven journey sessions** along each complete process (the only mode producing live-region and focus-indicator machine evidence at journey level); `playwright-spec` for keyboard, focus trap, zoom; `axe-core` on every state of every screen; `@guidepup/virtual-screen-reader` for computed names and announcements on the upload, timeout dialog, and error summary components; manual NVDA and VoiceOver sessions on P1 and P2 end-to-end | Evaluator, all of it. SC determinations are not delegated. Contractor supplies test account, staging, and a non-submitting application path. |
| **Training video library** | The player once (control inventory, keyboard operability of every control, **menu level of the caption control and the audio-description control relative to volume**); then per-video: caption presence, caption accuracy and sync, and what the "narrated version" actually is | `agent-browser` + `playwright-spec` for the player control inventory and real-key operability; **human watching** for caption accuracy/sync and audio description — no mode substitutes for it | Evaluator determines the player's 503.4.x outcome (one determination, all 40 videos). Agency QA runs the per-video watch queue against a fixed rubric we supply; evaluator adjudicates. |
| **Documents (~200 PDFs)** | Inventory and classification (worksheets / policy guidance / older annual reports / scans); then a sampled manual review: tagged structure, reading order, headings, alt text, table headers, form-field labels on fillable worksheets, and whether scans are image-only | **Manual / AT methods only.** Outside the web measurement stack; governed by E205.4 and its non-web-document exception, mapped to the Electronic Documents boundary (57 tests — a boundary, not a capability) | Agency QA builds the inventory and classification. Evaluator reviews the sample and makes determinations. Read the exact SC list of the E205.4 non-web-document exception off the verified reference before writing the document outcome map — several site-shaped criteria are relieved for non-web documents and must not be reported as document failures. |
| **Staff intranet** | *If G1 admits it:* same examination as the public site, on 4 templates + HR forms, plus the E205.3 category attribution per template | Same web modes as the public site, executed from inside the agency network | Evaluator, on agency-provided network access. Legal + 508 coordinator own the G1 determination. |

**On the APG references used throughout §5–§6:** the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide is informative, not normative. We use APG patterns as the yardstick for judging whether a widget's keyboard and state model is coherent. A deviation from APG is *evidence toward* a WCAG success criterion failure — it is never itself a Section 508 failure, and the report never states it as one.

---

## 5. Evaluation Content — structure, interaction, focus, state

### 5.1 Semantic structure (Phase 2)

Per sampled view: landmark completeness and uniqueness (`main`, `nav` with distinguishing labels, `banner`, `contentinfo`); heading hierarchy with no skipped levels; lists marked as lists; data tables distinguished from layout tables with header association; form grouping via `fieldset`/`legend` on the application's grouped inputs; skip-link presence, focusability, and whether its target actually receives focus. Floor SCs: 1.3.1, 1.3.2, 2.4.1, 2.4.6, 2.4.2. Baseline tests: `4.A-BypassBlocks` (covered), `11.A-PageTitled`, `12.A-DataTableRole`, `12.B-DataTableHeaderAssociation`, `12.C-LayoutTable`, `13.A-HeadingDescriptive`, `13.B-VisHeadingProg`, `13.C-ProgHeadingVisual`, `13.D-List`, `18.B-CSSPositionedContent`, `19.A-FrameTitle`, `19.B-iFrameName`, `23.A-MultipleWays`.

Note the shape of `12.B-DataTableHeaderAssociation`: automated rules validate association markup that *exists*. A data table with no header markup at all passes those rules in silence. Header absence on identified data tables is a human check, and the portal's status table is exactly the kind of table where this bites.

### 5.2 Interactive elements — APG yardstick, keyboard model, floor SC, baseline test

| Widget (to confirm in Explore) | Where | APG pattern used as yardstick | Keyboard model evaluated | State evaluated | Floor SC | Baseline test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary nav / dropdowns | Site, intranet | Disclosure (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/disclosure/) or Menu and Menubar (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menubar/) | Tab, Enter/Space, Esc, Arrows if menubar | `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` | 2.1.1, 2.4.3, 4.1.2 | `1.A`, `2.B`, `5.A`–`5.C`, `4.B` |
| County office locator | Site | Combobox (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/) for the search; map region is non-APG custom | Tab, Arrows, Enter, Esc | `aria-expanded`, active-option management, results announcement | 2.1.1, 1.3.1, 4.1.2 | `1.A`, `5.A`–`5.D`, `10.A` |
| News listing / carousel *(if present)* | Site | Carousel (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/carousel/) | Tab to pause control; Arrows | pause/stop/hide available and operable | 2.2.2 | `21.B`, `21.C` |
| Accordions on policy pages | Site, intranet | Accordion (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/accordion/) | Tab, Enter/Space | `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` | 4.1.2 | `5.C` |
| Multi-step application form | Portal | Native form semantics; step indicator judged against Tabs (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/) only if implemented as tabs | Tab, Enter, Arrows if tabbed | `aria-invalid`, `aria-describedby`, required marking, current-step indication | 1.3.1, 2.4.6, 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 3.3.3, 4.1.2 | `10.A`–`10.G`, `5.A`–`5.D` |
| Document upload | Portal | Button (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/button/) + native file input; any drag zone is an enhancement that must have a single-pointer equivalent | Tab, Enter/Space | constraints programmatically associated; progress/complete conveyed | 2.1.1, 1.3.1, 3.3.2 (floor); 4.1.3, 2.5.7 (recommendation) | `5.A`, `10.A`, `10.B` |
| Session timeout dialog | Portal | Modal Dialog (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialogmodal/) | Tab trapped, Esc, Enter to extend | `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, `aria-labelledby`, focus moved in and restored out | **2.2.1**, 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 4.1.2 | `21.A`, `1.B`, `2.B`, `5.A`–`5.C` |
| Status table (sortable) | Portal | Table (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/table/) | Tab, Enter/Space on sort controls | `th`/`scope`, `aria-sort`, sort state non-color | 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 4.1.2 | `12.A`, `12.B`, `5.C`, `7.A` |
| Reviewer message list | Portal | Native list; Feed (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/feed/) only if virtualized | Tab | unread state conveyed by more than color | 1.3.1, 1.4.1 | `13.D`, `7.A` |
| Media player toolbar + settings submenu | Video library | Toolbar (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/toolbar/) + Menu Button (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menu-button/) | Tab into toolbar, Arrows within, Enter/Space, Esc from menu | `aria-pressed` on CC/AD toggles, accessible names on all controls | 2.1.1, 4.1.2 **+ 508 503.4, 503.4.1, 503.4.2** | `17.A`, `17.B`, `17.C`, `5.A`–`5.C` |
| Shared login | Auth | Evaluated as encountered; not remediated | Tab, Enter | error identification, paste support | 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 2.1.1 (best-effort); 3.3.8 is 2.2-only recommendation | `10.A`–`10.F` best-effort |

### 5.3 Focus (Phase 4)

Per sampled view and along every complete process: tab order against visual reading order; keyboard traps; focus visibility measured, not eyeballed — kat's dual-signal focus-indicator measurement is the stack's only machine evidence of indicator sufficiency; focus behavior on portal step transitions (client-side routing moves the view but frequently leaves focus stranded at the top of the document or on a removed node); focus into and out of the timeout dialog; focus after validation failure (does it land on the error summary, on the first invalid field, or nowhere?); focus after upload completes; focus on in-page anchors in long policy pages. Floor SCs: 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 3.2.1. Baseline tests: `1.A-KeyboardAccess`, `1.B-NoKeyboardTrap`, `2.A-FocusVisible`, `2.B-FocusOrder`, `2.C-OnFocus`, `3.A-NonInterference`.

### 5.4 State communication (Phase 5)

| State | Where | Visual channel checked | Programmatic channel checked | Floor SC | Recommendation layer | Baseline test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Field invalid | Portal | border, icon, message text | `aria-invalid`, `aria-describedby` resolving to the message | 1.3.1, 3.3.1, 4.1.2 | — | `10.D`, `10.F` |
| Field required | Portal | asterisk / "required" | `required` / `aria-required` + text, not color alone | 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 3.3.2 | — | `10.E`, `10.B`, `7.A` |
| Current step | Portal | highlighted indicator | heading, page title change, or `aria-current` | 1.3.1, 2.4.2 | — | `11.A`, `13.A` |
| Upload in progress / complete | Portal | spinner or bar | announced status | *(no floor SC for the announcement)* | **4.1.3** | *none — see note* |
| Session expiring | Portal | countdown dialog | dialog role + focus move + announcement | **2.2.1**, 4.1.2 | 4.1.3 for the countdown | `21.A` |
| Submit disabled | Portal | greyed | `disabled` / `aria-disabled` | 4.1.2 | — | `5.C` |
| Message unread | Portal | bold or colored dot | text or accessible name | 1.3.1, 1.4.1 | — | `7.A` |
| Captions on/off, AD on/off | Player | icon state | `aria-pressed` | 4.1.2 | — | `5.C`, `17.A` |
| Accordion expanded | Site, intranet | chevron | `aria-expanded` | 4.1.2 | — | `5.C` |
| Search results loaded | Site | count text | live region | *(none)* | **4.1.3** | *none* |

**The rows with no baseline test are the delta made concrete.** 4.1.3 Status Messages is a WCAG 2.1 criterion; it is not in the Section 508 basis and the 62-test web baseline has no test for it. A screen reader user who uploads a document and hears nothing — no progress, no success, no failure — is plausibly the exact experience behind the complaint on file. That finding will be reported as a **CRITICAL-impact recommendation, not a Section 508 failure**, and the report will say so in those words. If it were quietly labeled a 508 violation, the contractor could correctly refuse it under the contract; if the impact severity were softened because it is "only a recommendation," the agency would learn nothing from its own complaint. Both errors are avoided by keeping the two dimensions orthogonal.

---

## 6. Visual, Content, and Media Evaluation (Phases 6, 7, 7b)

### 6.1 Contrast and color
`8.A-ContrastMinimum` (covered) — axe-measured ratios across all sampled views, with human sampling for gradient and image-backed text that automated measurement flags as indeterminate. `7.A-Color` (partial) — automation reaches only color-only link distinction; every other color-as-sole-means judgment (status colors in the portal table, required-field marking, unread indicators, chart or map legends in the office locator) is a human pass. Floor SCs: 1.4.3, 1.4.1.

### 6.2 Zoom and magnification — the answer to the web team's question

**Yes, it belongs in this engagement, and it splits across both layers. Do not let the split be read as "half of it doesn't matter."**

- **1.4.4 Resize Text at 200% is WCAG 2.0 AA — inside the floor.** Baseline test `22.A-ResizeText` (covered): `playwright-spec` zoom/reflow verification plus visual regression. If the portal breaks at 200%, that is a **Section 508 conformance failure**.
- **1.4.10 Reflow (400% / 320px equivalent) is WCAG 2.1 — outside the floor.** No baseline test exists. "Unusable zoomed in on small laptops" most likely lands here, and it will be reported as a recommendation with CRITICAL user impact if it blocks application completion.
- **And the evaluation looks past the label.** When zoom breaks a layout badly, floor criteria often break with it: reflow that reorders content breaks 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence; content that scrolls out of reach breaks 2.1.1 or 2.4.3; controls that overlap break 2.4.7. We test the magnification journeys at 200% and 400% and report whatever floor consequences we find, rather than filing the whole complaint under a criterion the contract does not reach.

Also in the recommendation layer here: 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, 1.4.12 Text Spacing, 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus, 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.5.8 Target Size.

### 6.3 Motion, flashing, audio
`21.B-MovingInfo` and `21.C-AutoUpdate` (partial — identifying moving content needs temporal human observation the scans do not do), `21.D-AudioControl` (partial), `9.A-Flashes` (**not covered** — flash-frequency analysis needs PEAT-class tooling the stack does not have; recon can only note that flashing content exists). Floor SCs: 2.2.2, 2.3.1, 1.4.2.

### 6.4 Images and text-as-image
`6.A-MeaningfulImage` and `6.B-DecorativeImage` (partial — presence is machine-checkable, equivalence of meaning is not), `6.D-ImageText` (**not covered** — no OCR in the stack). Relevant if program eligibility rules or deadlines are posted as graphics, which is common on program sites and worth a targeted look in Explore. Floor SCs: 1.1.1, 1.4.5.

### 6.5 Links, labels, language
`14.A-LinkPurpose` (partial), `10.B-FormDescriptiveLabel` (partial), `10.E-FormHasLabel` (covered), `15.A-LanguagePage` (covered), `15.B-LanguagePart` (partial — detecting unmarked language changes is human). Floor SCs: 2.4.4, 3.3.2, 3.1.1, 3.1.2.

### 6.6 Sensory characteristics and audible cues
`7.B-SensoryCharacteristics` and `7.C-AudibleCues` — **both not covered**, manual only. Instructions in application worksheets and guidance ("click the button on the right," "the box below") are exactly where this shows up on a forms-heavy product. Floor SCs: 1.3.3, 1.4.1.

### 6.7 Time-based media — where the clearest 508 finding probably lives

The player description in the brief points at a Section 508 provision that has no WCAG equivalent at all:

**508 503.4.1** requires the caption user control to be at the same menu level as the user controls for volume or program selection. **503.4.2** requires the same of the audio-description control. The brief describes captions and the narrated version sitting **two levels down inside a settings submenu, while play and volume sit on the main toolbar**. That is a **candidate failure of 503.4.1 and 503.4.2 — stated as a hypothesis to confirm by inspection, not as a finding**, and it is the single highest-value thing this evaluation will produce that a WCAG-2.2-only audit would never generate, because WCAG contains no such requirement at any version. Baseline tests: `17.A-MediaPlayerCCADControls`, `17.B-MediaPlayerCCLevel`, `17.C-MediaPlayerADLevel` (all partial — the control inventory is machine-collectable, the same-menu-level equivalence judgment is human). One player, one determination, applies to all 40 videos.

Per-video, on the sample:
- **Captions (1.2.2, WCAG 2.0 A — floor).** `17.D-CaptionsPrerecorded` (partial): caption-track presence is machine-flaggable; accuracy and synchronization require watching. "Captions exist for most videos" means the remainder are candidate failures — get the definitive list from the contractor rather than inferring it from the player.
- **Audio description (1.2.3 at Level A, 1.2.5 at Level AA — both floor).** `17.E-ADPrerecorded` — **not covered**; AD is often a separate audio mix invisible to the DOM, so presence and adequacy require listening. **The "separately recorded narrated version" must be classified before it can be credited**, and it has three possible readings with three different outcomes: (a) genuine audio description of visual-only information → satisfies 1.2.3/1.2.5; (b) a full media alternative for video → satisfies 1.2.3 only; (c) merely a different narrator reading the same script with no descriptive content → satisfies neither. We determine this per asset. We do not guess, and we do not take the contractor's label for it.
- **`17.F-CaptionsLive`** — expected **inapplicable** (no live content declared); confirmed in Explore and reported as `inapplicable`, not `untested`.
- **`16.A`–`16.D`** (audio-only, video-only, and media alternatives) — **all not covered**; applicability determined in Explore.

**Structural point worth naming to the agency: seven of the thirteen not-covered baseline tests are media tests.** The part of the product where the tooling helps least is also the part with 40 assets and a part-time QA person. That is a budget fact, not a tooling complaint, and it drives the media sampling depth in §10.

## 7. Execution and Coverage (Phase 8)

### 7.1 Testing layers and routing

Static analysis is not applicable — we do not have source access to the portal (confirm; if the contractor provides the React repo, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` becomes a useful pre-remediation gate for the contractor's own pipeline, though it produces no evaluation evidence). Runtime layers: `axe-core` for machine-decidable violations across all sampled states; `playwright-spec` for codified real-key keyboard, focus, and zoom/reflow assertions; `keyboard-a11y-tester` driven sessions for the four complete processes — the only mode producing machine evidence of focus-indicator sufficiency and journey-level live-region behavior; `@guidepup/virtual-screen-reader` for component-level computed names and announcements on the upload, timeout dialog, and error summary; `agent-browser` for reconnaissance inventories. Manual AT sessions (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) carry every judgment no tool can make.

**Calibration that keeps the report honest:** kat batch-crawl 4.1.3 findings are prompts to run a driven session, never failures on their own. The Playwright MCP is not used — its key presses are silently dropped. Virtual-screen-reader assertions are never keyboard-operability evidence; its interactions are synthetic.

The ~200 PDFs are not measured by the web stack under any mode (§1.4a). Caption accuracy, audio-description presence and adequacy, flash frequency, text-in-image, and audible cues are not measured by any mode. The shared login service is third-party and evaluated best-effort. Every one of these appears in the report's coverage boundary section by name, with the method that covers it instead. None of them is ever reported as though automation touched it.

## 8. Standing Answers for the Web Lead, the Coordinator, and Procurement

### 8.1 The HTML checker

The web lead is right to care about markup quality and wrong about where it lands in this report. Three reasons, then the arrangement that gives them what they actually want:

1. **The federal test process itself does not test parsing.** Baseline test `24.A-Parsing` always passes by upstream design — the instruction reads "No testing necessary," following WCAG 2.0 Errata 13. We will not manufacture failures under a test the government's own process declares non-testable.
2. **WCAG 2.2 removed 4.1.1 Parsing entirely.** Neither the floor's test process nor the recommendation target supports "validator error = accessibility violation."
3. **Most validator errors have no user consequence.** An unrecognized attribute on a custom element does not affect any assistive technology.

**What we do instead — routing, not dismissal.** Every validator error gets triaged, and errors with real consequences are reported under the criteria they actually break: duplicate `id` values that break `aria-describedby` or `aria-labelledby` resolution → 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 (baseline `5.A`, `5.C`, `10.D`); mis-nested interactive elements that corrupt name or role computation → 4.1.2 (`5.A`, `5.B`); unclosed elements that change reading order → 1.3.2 (`18.B`); duplicate or missing form control associations → 1.3.1 and 3.3.2 (`10.A`, `10.E`).

**The arrangement:** the web lead gets a **validator triage appendix** listing every error the checker reports with an explicit disposition — *routed to SC X and filed as finding N* / *no user consequence, no finding* / *already remediated*. Nothing is silently dropped, the web team can see exactly what happened to each line, and the contractor's fix list stays defensible when they push back. What the appendix will not do is put validator output into the conformance map, because a report that inflates markup noise into legal violations is one the contracting officer cannot use.

### 8.2 The WCAG 2.2 assumption

The vendor's statement is half true, and the half that is false is the half that matters here.

True: WCAG 2.2 is the current W3C Recommendation. False: that older versions "don't matter." **The contract names Revised Section 508 as the legal authority, and Revised Section 508 incorporates WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA.** The regulation sets the floor, not the W3C's release calendar. A newer version of a standard does not retroactively amend the regulation that incorporated the older one.

Testing and reporting to 2.2 instead would break the deliverable in both directions at once:

- **Over-claim.** It would label 2.1 and 2.2 criteria — Reflow, Status Messages, Target Size, Accessible Authentication — as Section 508 failures. They are not, the contractor could correctly refuse them under the contract, and the report's credibility would not survive the first challenge.
- **Under-claim.** It would silently drop everything in the 508 basis that WCAG 2.2 does not contain: 4.1.1, and — more consequentially — the non-WCAG provisions. **The caption and audio-description control-placement requirements (503.4.1, 503.4.2) exist nowhere in WCAG at any version.** A 2.2-only audit of this product would very likely miss the cleanest 508 failure it has.

**So: report against the floor, recommend against WCAG 2.2 AA, declare the delta in both directions in the same report, visibly separated.** The web team loses nothing they wanted — WCAG 2.2 AA is still the remediation target we hand the contractor, and the modern criteria still reach the contractor's fix list carrying full user-impact severity. What changes is only which column of the report they sit in, and that column is what makes the report usable by a contracting officer.

### 8.3 "Does your testing approach carry official government approval or a stamp?"

**No. Plainly no, and here is exactly what we are not claiming:**

- We do not describe our process as "baseline-aligned" or "baseline-conformant." Baseline alignment recognition is an **external review of a test process**, not a badge a vendor declares about itself.
- No one on this engagement holds **DHS Trusted Tester certification**, and that credential is held by individual humans — never by a tool, a script, or a methodology. We do not claim it directly or by implication.
- **Nothing we produce is an ACR or a VPAT**, and no artifact should be presented as one.

What we offer instead is the itemized, verifiable coverage statement in §7.2: what our execution modes are designed to cover against the 62 active web tests, what they partially cover, and the 13 named gaps assigned to manual and AT methods. A reviewer can check every line of that against the published baseline. A stamp cannot be checked, because we do not have one.

**If the agency needs certified execution or a signed ACR, say so now.** Trusted Tester-certified execution is a different staffing requirement, and an ACR is normally authored by the offeror. Both are procurement actions that belong in week 1, not week 11.

### 8.4 Can the PDFs and the intranet ride along in the same automated pass?

**These are two different questions with two different answers, and collapsing them is the mistake to avoid.**

**PDFs: no — this is a capability boundary, not a scheduling problem.** No configuration of the web stack evaluates a PDF. Documents are governed by E205.4 and its non-web-document exception, map to the Electronic Documents baseline (57 tests — a declared boundary, not a capability), and are assigned to manual and AT methods with sampled human review. The scanned files are the sharpest case: an image-only scan has no text layer for any tool or assistive technology to reach. Adding PDFs to the crawl would produce nothing except a scan log that falsely implies coverage. Before writing the document outcome map, read the exact success-criterion list of the E205.4 non-web-document exception off the verified reference — several site-shaped criteria are relieved for non-web documents and must not be reported as document failures.

**Intranet: technically yes, procedurally not yet.** The intranet is web content the stack can measure with the same modes as the public site. Two things block it, neither of them tooling: (1) **gate G1** — the E205.3 determination from counsel about which content is agency official communication; sampling before that determination means sampling content that may be out of scope while missing content that is in it; (2) **network access** — the scan must run from inside the agency network, which needs the coordinator's arrangement. Clear both and the intranet joins the ordinary web lane in week 4. Miss G1 by week 3 and the intranet is declared out of scope with a stated limitation, per §1.4.

## 9. The Deliverable (EM Step 5 / Phase 9)

### 9.1 Report structure — three readers, one of them technical

Built on the A11y Evaluation Report Contract, layered so the program director and contracting officer can stop after section 2 and the coordinator and contractor can work from sections 3–6.

1. **Outcome summary (1–2 pages, plain language, no jargon).** What we evaluated, what an applicant can and cannot do today, what the highest-impact problems are, what changes before renewal. Written for the program director and the contracting officer.
2. **Declarations.** Conformance target (the floor, verbatim), product scope with the in/out rule per part, the accessibility support baseline, the sample set with rationale and the random-selection method, and the coverage boundary naming everything the web stack could not measure.
3. **Per-success-criterion outcome map against the declared floor.** Every WCAG 2.0 A/AA criterion plus the named non-WCAG provisions, each marked **passed / failed / cantTell / inapplicable / untested**, with at least one concrete example for every failed criterion. `inapplicable` and `untested` are distinct and both are used honestly.
4. **Findings**, each carrying the evidence finding contract with `evaluation_context` linking it to its sample, `section_508_fpc_context` where Chapter 3 FPC applies via E204, and the optional `baseline_test` field. Each finding carries a user-impact severity — **CRITICAL / MAJOR / MINOR / ENHANCEMENT** — assigned independently of its conformance outcome, with the two shown side by side so neither can be read off the other.
5. **Recommendations against WCAG 2.2 AA**, in their own section, explicitly labeled as recommendations rather than Section 508 conformance failures — and carrying their own impact severity, because "recommendation" is a legal classification, not a priority.
6. **Appendices:** the federal annex (below), the validator triage appendix (§8.1), and the evidence index.

### 9.2 What procurement attaches to the contract file

- The evaluation report, complete with its declarations and coverage boundary.
- **The federal annex** — per-baseline-test outcomes across the 62 active web tests. This is the direct answer to "which of the government's required tests did your process perform." **Deliverable boundary: the annex is evidence FOR whoever authors an Accessibility Conformance Report. It is not an ACR or a VPAT and must never be presented as one.**
- The evidence package: axe-core JSON per sampled view and state, kat traces / findings / reading-order census per complete process, `playwright-spec` results, zoom and focus screenshots, AT session notes, the media review log, and the document review log.
- The signed accessibility support baseline and the signed product-scope declaration, including the G1 outcome.

One sentence the contracting officer should carry into the renewal conversation: **this package documents that the product was tested and what the testing found. It does not certify that the product conforms.** Those are different claims, and only the first is one we can make.

## 10. Schedule, Gates, and Drop Order

| Weeks | Work | Owner | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Explore (five lists); draft all EM Step 1 declarations; review the complaint file; request test account, staging, non-submitting application path; brief the web lead on §8.1–8.2 | Evaluator; coordinator; contractor | — |
| 2 | **G1: written E205.3 intranet determination** | Counsel + coordinator | Miss by wk 3 → intranet out, limitation stated |
| 2 | **G2: portal test account + staging + non-submitting path** | Contractor | Miss by wk 3 → escalate to the contracting officer; P1–P3 cannot be evaluated without it |
| 3–4 | Sample selection + written rationale; batch scans (site, portal, intranet if in) | Evaluator | Baseline declaration ratified |
| 5 | Representativeness check #1; expand structured sample if needed | Evaluator | — |
| 5–7 | Complete processes P1–P3: kat driven sessions, keyboard specs, NVDA and VoiceOver end-to-end | Evaluator | 🔍 **Checkpoint 1** |
| 6–8 | Media lane: player 503.4.x determination; caption/AD sample review | Evaluator + agency QA | 🔍 **Checkpoint 2** |
| 7–9 | Document lane: inventory, classification, sampled manual review | Agency QA + evaluator | — |
| 9 | Public site completion; intranet lane if in scope; P4 | Evaluator | — |
| 10 | Consolidation; per-SC outcome map; federal annex; severity assignment | Evaluator | 🔍 **Checkpoint 3** |
| 11 | Draft to the 508 coordinator; validator triage appendix to the web lead | Evaluator | — |
| 12 | Final report + evidence package | Evaluator | — |

**Sampling depths that fit this timeline and this staffing:** ~30 web views structured + 3 random; 4 complete processes; **12 of 40 videos** for caption accuracy and audio-description classification (structured by video type + random, with the player determination covering all 40); **25 of ~200 documents** (structured by the four document classes + random).

**Pre-agreed drop order if a gate slips, decided now rather than in week 11:** (1) intranet lane; (2) representativeness iterations beyond the first; (3) document sample 25 → 12; (4) video sample 12 → 6. **Never dropped:** processes P1 and P2, the media player 503.4.x determination, and the per-SC outcome map against the floor. Anything dropped is reported as `untested` with the reason — never as `passed`, and never as silence.

### Where our confidence is lowest

Three places, stated so nobody is surprised. The **12-week timeline against this staffing** is the weakest part of this plan; the depths above fit, but they leave no absorption for a G1 or G2 slip. The **audio-description classification** (§6.7) could go three ways per asset and we will not know until we watch. And **the complaint's actual root cause is unknown** — the upload-status hypothesis in §5.4 is a plausible illustration, not a diagnosis, and if the true cause sits inside the other agency's shared login service, this evaluation can document it but this agency cannot remediate it.
